Examples include: demo 1 adding vertical gaps between repeated marks in columns 2, 6, and 13 and horizontal gaps at row 16; demo 2 completing short gaps in the top/bottom horizontal outline, left/right outline columns, and an interior marked column; demo 3 filling gaps along several repeated vertical columns and horizontal rows; demo 4 likewise completing short outline gaps and repeated interior-column gaps. These examples support a collinear-gap completion family, but the selector is **not** fully specified by “connect every same-color pair”: very long gaps between opposite frame sides are left untouched, and the accepted test has one selected interior column rather than horizontal fills through every row. Distinguish which aligned marks/segments form intended lines from incidental frame alignments. Do not infer a universal distance cutoff from these examples. If a future instance has multiple plausible eligible alignments, request a demo only if it can distinguish the selector; otherwise use the strongest repeated-alignment pattern and preserve unselected cells.

Operational checklist for this recurrence: record all marker coordinates and connected structures; identify collinear repeated markers/segments; compare demo deltas including untouched alignments; write 2 only into demo-supported gaps, keeping marker colors and all unrelated cells. Mechanically validate dimensions/rows. This newer accepted case is separate from and does not erase earlier `task-e6aa86dd` evidence for filling missing cells on a marker bounding-box perimeter; inspect each fresh input and any demos rather than assuming one single behavior for the task ID.

## Recurring task evidence: task-e1508c2c, translate the entire foreground pattern down one row

One demo and one accepted fresh test establish a simple one-cell downward translation of all foreground cells, with the original positions cleared to the background. In the demo, background was 8 and foreground was 5 on an 8×21 grid. Every 5 in input row `r` appeared at the same column in output row `r+1` (for rows that fit); output row 0 was entirely background. The bottom input row had no foreground cells, so there was no clipping ambiguity. This is a global translation of the complete foreground pattern, not movement of one selected component: disconnected clusters and isolated pixels all shifted together.

Accepted fresh test: 29×27, background 3, foreground 9. Move every input 9 from `(r,c)` to `(r+1,c)`, preserving its column; initialize output as all 3s, so row 0 is cleared and original foreground locations are vacated, while all translated foreground cells are 9. Input foreground occupied rows 5–21, so all translated cells fit and no clipping was needed. The accepted output was generated mechanically and validated as 29×27 with values 0–9. Re-identify background/foreground colors per instance; the evidence directly supports a downward shift by exactly one row, not wraparound or any other direction. If a future instance has foreground on the final row, clipping behavior is not independently established.

### Accepted contrasting recurrence: task-e1508c2c, unchanged 25×5 input

A fresh 25×5 instance was accepted with the output exactly equal to the input (no demos, no wrong submissions). The grid was all 5 except for a 5×5 patch of mostly 6s at rows 9–13, with a 5-valued hole at `(10,3)` (0-based), and an isolated/attached 6 at `(14,2)`; all remaining cells were 5. This differs from the earlier instances where a clearly identified foreground pattern translated down one row. Treat this as a genuine accepted no-op case, but do not infer a new general rule from this single example: it may represent a distinct latent branch/structure under the recurring task ID. For future instances, test whether a one-row shift is warranted by the current geometry and any demos; do not assume every task-e1508c2c input must move, and preserve the full grid when evidence supports a no-op.

### Further demo-supported and accepted recurrence: task-e1508c2c, whole-grid downward shift

A fresh 29×23 test was solved with two demos and zero wrong submissions. The accepted rule for this instance was to shift the entire non-background pattern down exactly one row, preserving columns, clearing the top row to background, and clipping anything that would move below the bottom edge. Test background was 8 and foreground 7; all 7s moved from `(r,c)` to `(r+1,c)`. Mechanically generated output was dimension-checked and accepted.

Demo 1 (19×28) used background 1 and foreground 8: every 8 moved down one row, with row 0 remaining all 1; all input 8s fit after translation. Demo 2 (20×12) used background 2 and foreground 9: the entire grid content shifted down one row, output row 0 was all 2, output rows 1–19 equaled input rows 0–18, and the old bottom row was clipped. This second demo directly clarifies bottom-edge behavior and shows that the translation applies to the whole pattern rather than a particular connected object. For new instances, identify the background and translate all foreground cells from the current input; keep the earlier accepted no-op 25×5 recurrence as a warning that task ID alone may not decide whether a shift applies—inspect current structure and use demos when the branch is ambiguous. Exact accepted test serialization had 29 rows × 23 columns and values 0–9.

### Further accepted recurrence: task-e1508c2c, 19×28 downward translation

A fresh 19×28 instance was solved with one demo and no incorrect submissions. The demo (24×4) had background 4 and foreground 2: output row 0 remained background, and each input foreground cell at `(r,c)` appeared at `(r+1,c)`, while the source position was cleared; all foreground fit. In the test, background was 8 and foreground was 2. Apply the same global one-row downward shift to every 2-valued cell, preserving columns and clearing row 0 to 8; the former bottom row is clipped. The input's final row was entirely background, so this test itself did not exercise foreground clipping. Accepted output retained 19×28 dimensions and was exactly `out[0]=[8]*28`, `out[r]=input[r-1]` for `r=1..18`. This provides another palette/shape confirmation of the downward-shift branch. The task ID also has an accepted no-op recurrence and prior shift examples; inspect the fresh geometry/demo rather than assuming every instance with this ID must shift.

A further reliability note: coordinates are 0-based in the stored translation description; when constructing, create a background-filled output and write each foreground cell at row `r+1` if in bounds. This avoids unintended wraparound and preserves all non-foreground/background cells when the input is truly binary.


## Recurring task evidence: task-67364822, replicate a populated panel pattern


A demo and accepted fresh tests establish a congruent-region replication transform. Identify complete separator lines and infer which congruent regions are repetitions of the same template. Copy non-background motif cells at identical local row/column offsets into corresponding blank regions; preserve the source, panel backgrounds, and separator lines. In one recurrence, a single populated 7×2 panel supplied the motif for all congruent panels. In another, the template was a whole 7×5 band whose motif was distributed across both sides of an internal vertical separator; repeat that band-pattern across the top and bottom bands, retaining the internal rail. Thus not every separator necessarily partitions the template into independently replicated panels: determine the repeated-region axis from the current layout and evidence. Do not treat separators as motif or fill background cells.

Demo (9×5): separator row 4 and column 2 split the grid into four 4×2 panels. Panel background was 5; the bottom-right panel contained 7 at local offset (0,0) and 6 at local offset (2,1). The output repeated these values at the same local offsets in all four panels: 7 at `(0,0),(0,3),(5,0),(5,3)` and 6 at `(2,1),(2,4),(7,1),(7,4)` (global coordinates zero-based). Existing source cells were preserved; separators remained 3.

Accepted fresh test (20×7): full-width separator rows of 3 at rows 6 and 13 split the grid into three equal 6×7 panels. The bottom panel was the source; its non-background motif was `[[2,2,2,2,2,5,7],[2,2,2,2,7,2,2],[2,2,2,2,2,5,2],[2,2,2,2,2,2,2],[2,6,5,2,2,2,2],[2,6,2,2,2,2,2]]` with panel background 2. Repeated that panel into rows 0–5 and 7–12 at the same local offsets, retaining the original bottom panel and both separator rows. The accepted output has three copies of the panel motif, with separator rows unchanged. Re-detect panel geometry, background, and source motif for each fresh instance; evidence supports congruent panels with one populated source, not arbitrary unequal partitions or conflicting motifs.

### Further accepted recurrence: task-67364822, replication across a 3×3 panel array

A fresh 17×11 test was solved after one demo and two incorrect submissions. Full separator rows of 4 at rows 5 and 11 and full separator columns of 4 at columns 3 and 7 (zero-based) partitioned the grid into a 3×3 array of congruent 5×3 panels. The background was 1. The sole source motif was in the middle-left panel, at local offsets `(0,2)=7`, `(1,0)=9`, and `(2,1)=7` (within panel rows 6–10, columns 0–2). Copy exactly those non-background cells to the same local offsets in every one of the nine panels, including the source; preserve all 4-valued separator rails and all other 1s. Accepted output retained 17×11 dimensions.

A demo for this same fresh instance had an 11×5 grid, separator rows of 2 at rows 3 and 7 and separator column 2, forming a 3×2 array of 3×2 panels. Background was 1. The top-left source motif was `(0,0)=6`, `(1,0)=8`, with the other cells background. The output copied those positions into all six panels. This directly confirms replication along both axes, not merely across the panel row containing the source.

Failure audit: the first wrong test submission replicated the pattern horizontally only within its source panel row and left the other two panel rows blank. The next wrong submission did replicate across all panels but shifted the motif down one local row; binary rejection gave no indication which issue remained. For each fresh grid, locate the exact source offsets relative to the panel's top-left, then replicate those offsets in both panel dimensions. Do not infer vertical offset from a nearby separator or blank margin; confirm the source panel bounds and exact local coordinates. Re-check every row width and all rails before serialization. Multiple-conflicting-source and nonuniform-background behavior remain untested.

### Further accepted recurrence: 9×19 four-quadrant replication, lower-left source

A test with no demos and no wrong submissions had full separator row 4 and full separator column 9, both 8, creating four 4×9 panels. Panel background was 4 and the lower-left panel contained the source. Copy all non-4 cells at identical local offsets into every panel, preserving rails; this includes several zero-valued cells, which are motif data rather than panel background. Exact source offsets/values: `(0,3)=7,(0,4)=0,(0,7)=6; (1,0)=5,(1,5)=0,(1,6)=0; (2,2)=9,(2,4)=6,(2,5)=1,(2,7)=6; (3,0)=0,(3,1)=1,(3,7)=5`. Output remained 9×19. This reinforces the 4-panel copy rule with a lower-left template and meaningful zeros; it does not resolve conflicting sources or unequal panels.

## Recurring task evidence: task-51a4dd40, recolor the trailing gap after a partial horizontal stripe

A demo and accepted fresh test support a simple row-local transform: in rows containing a solid horizontal stripe of one color that ends before the right edge, preserve that stripe and recolor the entire suffix to its right (which is uniform background in the evidence) to color 1. Rows whose stripe spans the full width remain unchanged; rows without the stripe remain unchanged. This is not a global recoloring of the background or a vertical continuation rule. Re-identify stripe/background colors per instance and locate the partial stripe row(s) from the current grid.

Demo (14×20): stripe color 8, background 4. Row 9 (0-based) had 8 in columns 0–15 and 4 in columns 16–19; the suffix became four 1s. A separate full-width row of 8 remained unchanged, as did all other rows.

Accepted fresh test (10×13): stripe color 3, background 6. Rows 4 and 8 were partial stripes: row 4 had 3 in columns 0–10, so columns 11–12 became 1; row 8 had 3 in columns 0–7, so columns 8–12 became 1. Full-width 3 rows 0 and 2 remained unchanged, and rows without a 3 stripe were preserved. No demos beyond the first were needed; zero wrong submissions. Evidence currently supports only horizontal stripes whose colored segment begins at the left edge and leaves a uniform suffix; do not extrapolate to interior gaps, stripes starting mid-row, other orientations, or suffixes containing mixed colors without further demos.

### Further accepted recurrence: task-51a4dd40, 11×15

A fresh 11×15 test was solved with zero demos and zero wrong submissions. The stripe color was 5 and the background was 4. Rows 0 and 6 had a left-edge run of seven 5s (columns 0–6), followed by eight 4s; recolor the suffix, columns 7–14, to 1. Row 9 had thirteen 5s (columns 0–12), followed by two 4s; recolor columns 13–14 to 1. Row 3 was a full-width 5 stripe and remained unchanged. All other rows contained only 4 and remained unchanged. Accepted output preserves 11×15 dimensions. This confirms that multiple partial stripes can occur, their suffix lengths may differ, and the entire right-hand suffix—not a fixed-size gap—is changed to 1; full-width stripes remain untouched. Re-identify stripe/background colors and the left-edge run length in each fresh input.

### Additional recurrence evidence and correction: task-51a4dd40 includes patterned suffixes

Later demonstrations and a fresh accepted test show that the initial “left-edge solid stripe with a uniform trailing suffix” description is too narrow for this task ID. Preserve that behavior as a demonstrated subcase, but do not assume all trailing areas are uniform or that every partial stripe should be changed. The task can also mark selected cells in patterned continuations with color 1, while leaving the interleaved cells and the rest of the grid unchanged.

Evidence from subsequent demos (colors/coordinates 0-based):
- Demo 3 (13×21; field 2, pattern color 5): unchanged upper pattern area; in lower rows, output adds 1s only in the far-right continuation. Row 10 changes c14,c15,c17,c18,c20 to 1; row 12 changes c16,c19 to 1. Other cells, including the alternating/intervening 2s, remain as input. This is not a general “replace the whole suffix” operation.
- Demo 4 (8×15; field 8, pattern color 6): only the lower repeated area is extended. Row 5 changes c5,c7,c9,c11,c13 to 1, leaving alternating 8s; row 6 changes c5–14 to 1. The corresponding upper pattern rows remain unchanged.
- Demo 5 (20×24; field 2, pattern color 9): only a small right-side continuation changes: row 2 c20,c22 become 1; row 3 c21,c23 become 1. All other cells stay unchanged. This is patterned/staggered, not a solid suffix.
- Demo 6 (11×16; field 0, stripe color 4) confirms the simple subcase: in rows 0, 3, and 10, the initial 4-run ends before the right edge and the entire remaining 0 suffix becomes 1; full-width stripe row 6 and all non-stripe rows are unchanged.

Fresh accepted test (12×24; colors 3/8): the accepted output changes only row 7 columns 20 and 22, and row 8 columns 19, 21, and 23, from 3 to 1. All other cells remain unchanged. In particular, the tempting leftmost partial/noisy rows 0–1 were NOT selected. A first submission recolored the wrong area (rows 0–1 were preserved in the accepted output); its rejection was a selector/scope error, not evidence that the color-1 mapping was wrong. This is a crucial negative example against applying the original left-edge-run rule indiscriminately.

Operationally: analyze the repeated stripe/pattern geometry in the current grid, identify the lower/right continuation cells actually selected by the pattern, and preserve unrelated partial rows and interleaved background cells. Use demos when it is unclear which pattern continuation is targeted. The exact generic selector for the patterned subcases is not fully determined by these notes; do not extrapolate a universal period/phase from one instance. In all demonstrated variants, newly marked cells are 1 and original pattern cells are preserved. Validate changed coordinates and output dimensions before submission.

A further 23×17 test for this ID remained unsolved after all eight demos and eight rejected submissions. Its input had two patterned bands, including solid-prefix rows and alternating 3/7 rows; neither filling only the solid row suffixes nor applying suffix completion to all trailing background rows was accepted. The output selector remains uncertain; preserve this as negative evidence and consult `references/task-51a4dd40-unresolved-variation.md` before future attempts. Several invalid-grid responses also resulted from hand-transcribed rows being short; generate and verify every row mechanically.

### Further recurrence: task-3af739a9, horizontal guide with narrow vertical motif

A further demo and accepted fresh test add evidence but leave the motif-placement rule geometry-dependent. In the demo (30×22), background was 4; full row 8 (0-based) was the color-2 guide; a 2×3 block of 9s occupied rows 14–16, columns 5–6. The output moved this motif upward to rows 9–11, columns 5–6, directly below the guide, and painted full row 12 color 8, immediately beyond the motif on its far side. The guide remained unchanged.

The accepted fresh test was 14×26 with background 0, full row 0 color 2, and an irregular color-1 motif with bbox rows 4–8, columns 3–8. The accepted output preserved the motif in place and added full row 9 color 8 immediately below its bottom edge; all other cells, including the guide, remained unchanged. A separate accepted 25×18 recurrence with a single horizontal stripe moved the stripe adjacent to the guide and placed a full color-8 line just beyond its far edge, clearing the original stripe. Together, evidence confirms adding the 8-line on the motif side opposite the guide, but does not support a universal instruction to translate the motif adjacent to the guide: some compact motifs/stripes move, while irregular or broad patterns remain in place. For future recurrences, re-identify line orientation and motif geometry, and do not assume either universal preservation or universal translation; fit actual demos or current geometry. Exact accepted test dimensions for this case were 14×26; one changed full row (row 9, all 26 cells) was 8.

### Further accepted recurrence: task-e1508c2c, sparse 27×11 downward shift

A fresh 27×11 test was accepted with zero demos and zero wrong submissions. Background was 7 and all foreground cells were 5. The complete foreground pattern (including its disconnected groups and isolated cells) shifted down exactly one row, preserving columns; row 0 remained all 7 and every source 5 was cleared as the pattern moved. The input foreground rows were 14–21 (0-based), so the translated pattern occupied rows 15–22 with no clipping. Row-wise foreground columns in the input were: r14 `{5}`; r15 `{5,6,7,9,10}`; r16 `{1,2,4,6,7,8,9}`; r17 `{1,3,4,5,6,7}`; r18 `{1,2,5,6,7,8}`; r19 `{2,3,6}`; r20 `{7,8,9}`; r21 `{10}`. ### Further accepted recurrence: task-e1508c2c, 11×20 patterned field

One demo and zero wrong submissions established a full-grid one-row downward shift for a fresh 11×20 test. Demo input was 15×20 with colors 2 and 5; demo output row 0 was all 5, and for every subsequent row `r`, output row `r` exactly equaled input row `r−1`. Thus the operation translates the complete canvas content downward, preserving columns and all colors, rather than selecting only one connected component. The old bottom row is clipped; the demo's final row was all background, so clipping of non-background cells was not exercised there.

The accepted 11×20 test used colors 3 and 5. Its output was exactly row 0 filled with 5, followed by input rows 0–9 in output rows 1–10; the original input row 10 was clipped. This was mechanically represented as `out[0]=[5]*20`, `out[r]=input[r-1]` for `r=1..10`. The pattern looked like a large irregular 3-valued region on a 5-valued field, but the demo supports translating whole rows/grid, not moving a selected component. This instance reinforces the downward-shift branch while the task ID still has an accepted no-op recurrence: use a demo when the current structure does not clearly select the applicable branch, and do not assume every task-e1508c2c input shifts.

### Further accepted recurrence: task-e1508c2c, 6×17 two-cell vertical pattern

A fresh 6×17 test was accepted after one demo request and zero wrong submissions. The demo was 17×10 with background 8 and two foreground 0 cells at `(5,1)` and `(6,2)` (0-based); in the output they appeared at `(6,1)` and `(7,2)`, respectively, with their original positions cleared. Thus the demonstrated operation is a global one-row downward translation, preserving columns and shape; the rest of the grid remained background. In the test, background was 5 and the two foreground 4 cells formed a vertical pair at `(2,3)` and `(3,3)`. The accepted output moved them to `(3,3)` and `(4,3)`, leaving all other cells 5. This gives direct evidence for applying the shift even to a tiny two-cell vertical component. As with other task-e1508c2c recurrences, retain the prior accepted no-op case as a reminder that the recurring task ID can branch; use the current demo and input evidence rather than the ID alone. Output dimensions remain unchanged; this test had no foreground on the bottom row, so it does not establish clipping behavior.

A fresh 16×16 instance was solved with one demo request and zero wrong submissions. Demo 1 (10×27; background 3, foreground 8) showed an exact downward shift of the complete canvas contents by one row: output row 0 was all 3; output rows 1–9 equaled input rows 0–8, preserving every column and both colors. The accepted test used background 4 and foreground 0, with sparse isolated 0s in the upper portion and a broad irregular 0 region lower down. # ARC action-grid serialization audit

## Reusable validation procedure

For large output grids, a correct transformation rule is not enough: the exact JSON action must encode the generated candidate, with the intended dimensions and every marked coordinate in the right row and column.

1. Parse input rows into a matrix and construct the output programmatically.
2. Validate height, every row width, and cell range. Check expected preserved cells and the exact set of changed coordinates.
3. Serialize the complete action object once, e.g. compact JSON from `json.dumps({"action":"submit","grid":out})`.
4. Submit that exact serialized object. Do not manually retype or visually reconstruct the rows afterward.
5. If the submission is rejected, compare the grid in the actual action against the saved/generated candidate cell-by-cell before revising the inferred rule. A mismatch means the intended answer and the submitted answer were not the same.
6. Never repeat an equivalent-looking hand-copied grid after rejection without first auditing exact row widths and changed coordinates. Binary feedback cannot locate the error.

## Session evidence and limitation

In a 14x25 test for a diagonal continuation task, the candidate was generated as a single diagonal of color 6 extending down-left from the existing aligned color-6 pair. Multiple submissions were rejected. Inspection of the tool-generated serialized candidates versus the final action objects shows the manually emitted grids did not consistently preserve the generated diagonal coordinates: some rows shifted the mark or omitted it. Thus these rejections do **not** establish that the inferred diagonal rule was wrong; the puzzle remained unresolved, and no accepted answer is claimed here. The durable lesson is to submit the exact generated JSON and audit the actual action after rejection, rather than cycling through rule hypotheses while output transcription remains unverified.

The demos in this instance also showed several geometries (diagonal rays, and rays extending from marker pairs toward a boundary), so this note is about serialization/debugging discipline only—not a generalized transformation rule. Re-derive task rules from the current demos.

# Boundary-aligned ray projection with interior markers

This is a demonstrated ARC transformation family: a repeated stripe/object along a grid edge establishes inward rays perpendicular to that edge. An interior marker color supplies the ray color; marker cells encountered along a ray become color 4. Preserve the edge source objects and unrelated cells. This pattern differs from copying a compact motif at scattered marker anchors: the edge structure defines ray orientation and placement, while marker-colored cells can stop/terminate rays.

## Evidence from a Continual-ARC instance

Three demos established a shared broad pattern, and the test transformation below was accepted. Coordinates are zero-based in these notes.

### Demo 1 (10x7, background 1)

- The input had color-3 pairs on the top edge at `(0,1..2)` and bottom edge at `(9,5..6)`, plus one color-2 interior marker at `(8,2)`.
- The output retained the color-3 edge pairs. It drew color 2 inward on columns 2 and 6: the top-edge pattern projected down column 2, ending at the marker; the bottom-edge pattern projected up column 6 across the grid. The marker at `(8,2)` became color 4. Unrelated cells were preserved.
- Output ray cells were `col 2, rows 1..7` and `col 6, rows 0..8`, with `(8,2)` changed to 4; the source cells stayed 3.

### Demo 2 (15x9, background 5)

- Color 8 occupied part of the right edge at rows 0..4, and part of the left edge at rows 10..14. Four singleton color-1 markers occurred in the lower-left region.
- The output retained the edge 8s and drew color-1 horizontal rays inward from the left-edge stripe on rows 10, 12, 13, and 14, ending at each marker; those markers became 4. The rays were respectively columns 1..4, 1..2, 1..5, and 1..3.
- The output also had color-1 horizontal bands from the right-edge stripe on rows 0, 2, 3, and 4, while row 1 remained unchanged. This example shows that not every cell in a contiguous edge stripe necessarily produces an observed ray; do not assume an unconditional per-cell extension rule without explaining such omissions from the task's full structure.

### Accepted test (10x6)

Input edge stripes were color 5: a left-edge vertical stripe on rows 0..3 and a right-edge stripe on rows 6..9. The interior marker color was 2. The accepted output preserved the edge 5s, painted inward horizontal rays with 2, and changed each encountered color-2 marker to 4:

- Rows 0..3: columns 1..5 became 2.
- Rows 6..9, from the right edge: fill color 2 leftward through each row's markers; the marker cell becomes 4. Specifically, row 6 marker at col 1; row 7 marker at col 2; rows 8 and 9 marker at col 1.
- Rows 4 and 5 and all unrelated cells remained unchanged.

## Applying this hypothesis safely

1. Identify repeated edge-aligned structures and their inward normal; verify whether opposite edge stripes create rays too.
2. Identify the ray color and any interior marker/stop color from demo deltas, not from color conventions.
3. Compare exact changed coordinates by row/column. Track rays that stop at a marker, reach an opposite boundary, or are absent despite a source cell; those distinctions are part of the rule, not noise.
4. Preserve source stripes and all unaffected cells. Change a marker to 4 only if the examples establish that convention.
5. Before spending another demo, name the unresolved distinction (e.g. why one stripe cell does not emit a ray) and consider whether it could change the test output. Do not generalize a per-edge-cell rule from one regular case when another demo contains an exception.

This case study supports the broad boundary-ray/marker behavior but leaves the full selection rule for the omitted top-right ray in Demo 2 unresolved. Treat that omitted-ray detail as a caution, not a universal parity or row-selection rule.

# Changed-object tasks: evidence ledger and hypothesis control

Use when demonstrations recolor one or more objects and the selection/replacement rule is not immediately clear.

## Evidence ledger

For each demo, capture:

| Demo | Exact changed cells/component | Original → new color | Shape/size | Candidate relation to unchanged objects |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Record all unchanged components that could be mistaken for a target as well. Identify objects by 4-connectivity unless diagonal connection is supported by the examples. Compare both bounding-box dimensions and exact normalized support shape; components with a similar color or size are not necessarily equivalent.

## Hypothesis discipline

1. State one concise rule that selects the changed object(s) and determines the replacement color.
2. Test that rule against every changed and unchanged object in every demonstration. Reject rules that explain only the salient output.
3. For the test, list candidate components and explicitly mark whether each satisfies the rule. Do not choose a plausible object merely because it can be recolored to a prominent color.
4. If multiple rules remain, identify what observation would distinguish them. Spend a demo only if its likely outcome separates the hypotheses and the budget permits.
5. When demos are exhausted, make one best-supported attempt. Avoid serially guessing one component/color pair per submission; this wastes attempts without adding information.

## Binary feedback and retries

A wrong answer eliminates the exact submitted grid, but does not say which assumption failed. Save the exact failed hypothesis in working notes, regenerate candidates from the original input, and change only a reasoned assumption at a time. Re-check parsing, component segmentation, selection criteria, replacement color, and any interaction between objects. Never treat an untested retry as a validated rule. If attempts remain and uncertainty is high, choose the next distinct candidate only when a demo-supported criterion favors it.

Keep the final action interface exact: one JSON action object only when required. Machine-check grid dimensions and row widths before submission.

This procedure is complementary to `references/rejected-candidate-audit.md`, which focuses on auditing stencil-copy submissions; this note covers changed-object selection/coloring tasks.

# Complete stencil extraction and validation

Use this when a source motif is matched against repeated patterns in the grid, including implicit targets that have no special marker.

## Extract the whole support

1. Record the source object's bounding box and transcribe every cell with coordinates; distinguish foreground/support from background or holes.
2. Normalize offsets relative to a fixed anchor only after the raw coordinates are recorded. Reconstruct the bounding-box crop from the extracted cells and verify no source cell was omitted or invented.
3. Do not substitute a visually salient line/component for an asymmetric multi-cell motif. Conversely, don't infer a larger bounding box by merging nearby unrelated noise.

## Validate against demonstrations

For each demo, calculate the exact input/output difference set. Translate the complete extracted support according to the proposed target rule and compare the predicted union to that difference set. A valid rule should account for every changed cell and produce no unexplained changes, while preserving unchanged/source cells as shown. If no candidate or too many candidates appear, revisit the extraction, anchor, target predicate, or color mapping rather than submitting a guess based on a partial stencil. Request another demo only when it can distinguish specific remaining hypotheses.

## Apply safely

Find all target placements against the original, unmodified input. Apply their transformed support as a union to a copy, then verify dimensions, row lengths, bounds, and the precise set of edits. This prevents cascading matches and catches accidental partial-stencil false positives.

This supplements `arc-grid-reasoning` and the implicit stencil search reference.

# Postmortem: repeated demo requests on an underdetermined recoloring task

This recurring task presented grids with many disconnected colored components. Eight demos showed one component changed per example, with widely varying colors, sizes, shapes, and replacement colors. Same-color components were often left unchanged. Those observations did not yield a stable selector or palette map.

## Lesson for future instances

- After each response, extract the exact input/output delta and update a positive/negative component ledger before taking another action.
- Keep selection and color mapping as separate hypotheses; test both against all changed and unchanged examples.
- Ask a demo only when a concrete competing pair of rules and a discriminating possible observation have been identified. Do not consume the full cap through generic requests while leaving the ledger unanalyzed.
- One rejected submission rules out only that whole output. It does not establish which component, color, or scope was mistaken. Avoid retrying near-identical guesses without a changed, evidence-backed hypothesis.
- Historical successful edits on a recurrence are test-specific evidence, not a universal selector. In particular, prior cases differ in test behavior, so don't copy a past target/color blindly.

No universal selector or mapping was established by the eight-demo case described here. Future work should treat a residual ambiguity as unresolved, rather than recording a guessed rule as reliable.

See also `references/changed-object-evidence-ledger.md` and `arc-demo-budget-strategy`'s `references/ledger-before-next-request.md` for general procedures.

# Demo-request discipline for ARC streams

Use this note when each extra demonstration costs an action and the instance has capped demos or attempts.

## After receiving a pair

1. Compare the new input/output difference, but do not reason from that pair in isolation. Reconcile it with every prior pair for the task.
2. Record the concise invariant: background and object roles, each changed region, preserved regions, and any unchanged lookalikes. Check exact cell coordinates when the task is ambiguous.
3. Keep only plausible hypotheses that explain both changed and unchanged cells across all examples. State what each predicts for the test.
4. Before requesting another pair, name the concrete uncertainty and what kind of example would resolve it. Ask only if that information could change the submitted output enough to justify its cost.
5. When a demo cap is nearly exhausted, do not let repeated requests replace analysis. Choose a best-supported transformation or request the final example only for a specific discriminating purpose.

## Common failure mode

Repeatedly requesting examples while describing the rule as underdetermined is not a useful fallback. It consumes the budget without establishing information gain and may leave no action for a supported answer. If a fresh pair still does not distinguish hypotheses, immediately update the ledger and decide whether another request is genuinely informative.

This is a decision procedure, not a claim that any particular grid transformation has been validated. Follow the task's exact action format and verify a candidate mechanically before submission.

# Demo rule synthesis: changed-object tasks

Use this when ARC examples show only a subset of objects changing and the rule is not immediately obvious.

## Evidence ledger

For every demo, record the input/output difference exactly, then summarize:

| Pair | Changed component cells / bounding box | Original color | New color | Nearby or distinctive structures |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Do not describe only the apparent motif: disconnected same-color pieces can be distinct objects, while adjacent cells of different colors may encode a larger relation. Record both 4-connected and 8-connected groupings when relevant.

## Hypothesis discipline

After each pair, state the rule that would select the changed object and map its replacement color. Keep at least two plausible hypotheses only when the evidence genuinely leaves them open. A hypothesis must explain every changed and unchanged object across all demos, not just one visually salient pair. Use a small table to check possible relations: shape match, size, color, position, adjacency, containment, object role, and relation to a larger marker/object.

Request another demo only when you can name the competing hypotheses it would distinguish. More examples are not automatically more useful; each request has a cost. Avoid repeated demo calls without doing the cross-example comparison first. Once evidence supports a rule, transform the test rather than spending requests indefinitely.

## Strict action interfaces

When a puzzle platform requires exactly one action JSON per turn, keep the response to that action. Make exactly one choice: request a demo, submit a grid, or finish if the instance is over. Do not include tool-call traces, reasoning prose, or multiple action objects in the puzzle response. Before submitting, validate the grid dimensions and all row lengths against the input.

This session did not establish a reliable task-specific mapping from its three demos; treat any guessed rule as unverified rather than recording a guessed transformation as fact.

# Edge-bounded line-art cavities: selection audit

## Reusable lesson

A 4-neighbor flood fill seeded from the grid boundary is useful for detecting fully enclosed blank components, but it is not a complete detector of intended fill targets. Some ARC demos select a window whose closure partly uses a canvas edge, or a blank gap defined by a line-art partition rather than a closed loop. Conversely, promoting every grid edge to a wall and filling every resulting bounded-looking bay can overfill: exterior corner/edge bays may remain unchanged.

## Reliable audit procedure

1. Identify the background and linework, then detect fully enclosed background components as initial candidates.
2. Inspect edge-adjacent candidate windows separately. For each, record its exact bounding box and bordering strokes; trace how the full line arrangement frames or partitions it.
3. Use the demos' unchanged areas as negative evidence. Distinguish an intentional window from an exterior bay, especially at corners or beyond the ends of strokes.
4. Recolor only the supported target cells; preserve linework and all other background. Verify exact changed coordinates mechanically.
5. After binary rejection, do not merely expand/shrink the same guessed fill. Re-audit every plausible window and the selector.

## Evidence from task-66859c98

Across demos, selected background patches were filled with color 4. Examples included enclosed windows, a left-edge-completed area, and a partition-like gap, so strict flood-fill enclosure was too narrow. In the test, however, treating all canvas edges as walls and filling all three apparent right-edge bays was rejected. The correct candidate was only the central 4x3 window (zero-based rows 5-8, columns 22-24), bounded by the horizontal strokes at rows 4 and 9, the vertical line at column 21, and the right canvas edge. Top and bottom right-edge bays remained background. This is case evidence, not a complete formal selector: use the whole geometric arrangement and changed/unchanged examples to infer intentional windows rather than applying a blanket edge rule.

## Budget and submission discipline

In a demo-capped stream, maintain an evidence ledger after each pair and request a new demo only for a concrete uncertainty that could change the output. Once demos are exhausted, select the best-supported candidate once. Emit exactly one action JSON when the interface requires it; do not expose analysis or tool traces in the response.

# Feedback-driven auditing and demo budgeting

Use this note after a plausible ARC candidate is rejected or when deciding whether to request more demonstrations.

## After a rejected candidate

Binary correct/incorrect feedback does not identify which assumption failed. Before retrying:

1. Regenerate the candidate from a fresh parse of the original grid; do not manually edit or retype the rejected output.
2. Compare the submitted grid and regenerated candidate cell-by-cell, including source-object handling, marker replacement, background-colored stencil cells, anchor alignment, orientation, clipping, and overlap precedence.
3. Change one evidence-based assumption at a time. Do not submit near-duplicates, and do not treat an untested alternative as a validated method.
4. Validate output dimensions, row widths, cell values, and serialization mechanically.

## Spend demo requests for information gain

A demo request is useful when it can distinguish concrete competing hypotheses, such as whether background-colored exemplar cells overwrite targets, which exemplar cell aligns with the marker, or whether the source exemplar is removed. If several examples already establish the broad transformation, another generic example may add little. Audit the failed candidate first; request a demo only if its likely result could change the next output. Include demo costs and remaining attempt budget in the decision.

# Implicit stencil search: complete support before scanning

Use this note when demonstrations suggest that a source motif is matched against background regions rather than copied at explicit marker cells.

## Reliable sequence

1. Record the entire distinctive motif, including every meaningful cell and its exact relative coordinate. Do not simplify an asymmetric or branched shape to its most obvious line/component.
2. Convert the source to a support mask: offsets of all non-background cells from a fixed anchor. Determine which cells constrain a match and which are background-colored holes only from demos.
3. Verify the full proposed support geometry and output color against each demonstration. The predicted placements must explain all changed cells; a partial motif can cause many false positives.
4. Scan valid translations against the untouched input. A candidate matches only if every constrained support cell meets the demonstrated background condition. No wrapping beyond grid bounds.
5. Collect all matches before editing. Apply transformed cells as a union where overlaps occur unless demonstrations establish precedence. This avoids edits cascading into new matches.
6. Preserve source and unrelated cells when examples show they remain unchanged. Mechanically validate dimensions, row widths, bounds, and generated output.

For a solid 1D motif of length L, enumerate all in-bounds segments whose L original cells equal background; overlapping segments are distinct matches and the output is their union. Do not use this shortcut for branched/multicolor stencils.

## Session lesson

A test contained a three-cell vertical color-1 exemplar, and the demonstrations showed every all-background vertical triple was recolored. The reusable algorithm is sound for that exact 1D support. The mistake to guard against is prematurely deciding that a motif is merely a line based on one visible component; another same-task demonstration had an irregular multi-cell motif. Always infer the complete task-specific stencil from all examples before scanning.

This is a detailed supplement to `arc-grid-reasoning` and `arc-stencil-replication`.

# Marker counts in separator-defined panels

A useful recurring ARC pattern partitions a grid into equal panels using complete separator rows and/or columns, then emits one output cell per panel. The output can encode the number of marker cells in each panel rather than copying marker positions.

## Evidence from two color/layout variants

- In one demo, the grid had 10 panels, each 4x2, with color 2 as panel background and color 9 as marker. The output was 2x5: the sole panel with one marker mapped to 2 (the background); all panels with two markers mapped to 1.
- In another demo, there were six 4x3 panels, color 9 as background and color 4 as marker. Its 3x2 output used 9 for panels with one marker and 1 for panels with two markers.

The shared mapping is therefore: one marker -> that task's panel background; two markers -> fixed output color 1. The marker colors and panel shapes differ, so infer rather than hard-code them.

## Application checklist

1. Find full separator rows/columns and establish exact panel bounds; exclude separators from marker counts.
2. Record the marker count for each panel in reading order and reshape into the output's panel arrangement.
3. Derive each count's output color from demos, including the background role. Do not assume output dimensions match input.
4. Check every demo panel, especially singleton/two-marker classes, before applying to the test.
5. Avoid extrapolating behavior for marker counts not shown by the demos.

This pattern is supported when all observed panels fall into the same demonstrated count classes. If they do not, consider additional features rather than forcing a count-only rule.

# Auditing a plausible but rejected ARC candidate

## When to use
Use after a submission is marked incorrect but the high-level transformation still seems supported by demonstrations. Binary correctness feedback does not reveal which assumption failed.

## Audit sequence

1. Re-parse the original grid and regenerate the candidate from that data; avoid manually patching a prior answer.
2. Check the full object bounding box, including background-colored cells/holes, and infer the anchor by matching exact relative offsets in each demonstration.
3. Independently verify whether the source exemplar is retained, removed, or transformed. Do not confuse preserving the source with painting its background cells into targets.
4. Check target marker replacement, transparent/background overwrite behavior, orientation/reflection, clipping at edges, and collisions/overlaps.
5. Compare candidate versus input cell-by-cell. Confirm all non-target cells that should remain fixed, all replicated pattern cells, row/column counts, and JSON structure.
6. If the same rule's close variants (such as source retained/removed) both fail, do not resubmit a near-duplicate. Identify the remaining assumptions and request a demonstration only if it could discriminate between them; otherwise reconsider object extraction or the rule itself.
7. Record confidence honestly: a failed candidate cannot establish which assumption was wrong, and an unverified alternative is not a validated procedure.

## Case note: unresolved 3x3 stencil

A task had background 4, a source array `[[4,5,5],[8,5,8],[8,5,0]]`, and scattered color-1 targets. Two generated candidates copied the stencil centered on targets, once without retaining the source and once retaining it; both were rejected. The demonstrations supported motif replication but binary feedback did not identify the faulty detail. This is an example of why coordinate regeneration and a systematic assumption audit are preferable to repeating a plausible pattern by intuition. Do not treat the case as evidence for a specific alternate rule.

## Checklist before retry

- [ ] Source object's exact bounding box and anchor are supported by demos.
- [ ] Every copied color, including 0 and any background-colored cell, has an explicit rule.
- [ ] Source handling and marker replacement are separately checked.
- [ ] Every candidate difference from the original is intentional.
- [ ] All dimensions and row widths are verified programmatically.
- [ ] The retry tests a concrete correction, not a guess indistinguishable from the failed output.

These notes supplement `references/stencil-copying.md`.

# Selected-component recoloring: evidence and unresolved observations

## Durable method

For a task that changes one among many disconnected shapes, record each 4-connected component separately with color, area, shape, position, and whether it changed. Also note components left untouched, especially same-color or similar-shaped candidates. Test candidate selection criteria against the entire ledger, not just the selected object. If useful, compare 8-connectivity to determine whether diagonal contacts affect object identity.

Keep selection and recoloring as separate inferences:

1. Which color class or object role is eligible?
2. Which component in that class changes (e.g. largest within a class versus largest overall)?
3. What determines its replacement color?

A hypothesis such as “the largest component of its color changes” only addresses question 2, and not necessarily why that color class was selected. Never assume it implies a palette mapping. Binary submission feedback cannot locate the wrong assumption, so avoid random candidate/color retries. Request a demonstration only when competing hypotheses are explicit and a new pair could distinguish them; otherwise conserve the demo budget.

# Exemplar-to-marker copying: worked notes

This reference summarizes a recurring ARC transformation class. A compact multicolor object is the exemplar; repeated isolated markers are target anchors. Demonstrations can establish both the motif and its anchor: e.g. a vertical 3-cell exemplar `[8,1,1]` copied to every marker with the marker replacing the middle cell, and a horizontal `[8,3,9]` copied with its middle cell aligned to each marker.

## Extraction and application

- Record the exemplar as a rectangular array, including cells matching the background. Record its source bounding box and likely anchor coordinate.
- For each target marker, translate each exemplar cell by `(target_row - anchor_row, target_col - anchor_col)`.
- Copy meaningful non-background colors; use transparent background cells unless the examples show backgrounds being painted.
- Keep the source exemplar unchanged if it remains present in demo outputs.
- Check edge targets: crop only out-of-bounds cells if the examples imply clipping; never wrap.

## Verification checklist

1. Does each demo target produce the exemplar's exact relative geometry and color order?
2. Is the marker at the exemplar's anchor, or does the marker replace some other cell?
3. Is the source exemplar preserved?
4. Are non-marker regions unchanged?
5. Do adjacent copies overlap? If so, verify precedence from examples.
6. Are dimensions and every row width unchanged?

A rejected submission despite a plausible copying rule should trigger a focused audit before another attempt: compare the submitted grid against input cell-by-cell; inspect possible source-object misidentification, anchor alignment, copied transparent/background cells, marker preservation, and transcription/serialization errors. Do not blindly repeat the same output or assume the conceptual rule is disproven.

## Session-specific diagnostic note

In one 3x3 stencil case, the source motif was `[[bg,5,5],[8,5,8],[8,5,0]]` on background 4, and targets were isolated color-1 cells. A generated stamp hypothesis can be plausible but an incorrect submission does not itself reveal which detail is wrong. Reconstruct the exact output mechanically from the input rather than hand-editing; compare source preservation, marker placement, and every row's dimensions. Treat any unverified alternative as a hypothesis, not established guidance.

# `task-51a4dd40`: unresolved fresh variation (12×24)

## Evidence from this instance

Two demos confirm a specific transformation for left-edge partial horizontal stripes:

- Demo 1 (11×13), background 2 and stripe color 3: rows 0, 5, and 8 had a left-edge run of 3 followed by a suffix of 2s. The suffix (respectively column 12, columns 6–12, and columns 3–12) changed to 1. Full-width 3 rows and rows without a qualifying prefix stayed unchanged.
- Demo 2 (21×19), background 5 and stripe color 7: row 14 had 7 in columns 0–8 followed by 5 in columns 9–18; row 19 had 7 in columns 0–15 followed by 5 in columns 16–18. Those suffixes changed to 1; the other rows stayed unchanged.

The fresh test is structurally different: it has fragmented 8/3 patterns in rows 0–1 and 7–8, with broad full-3 separator bands. It has no row consisting of a uniform left-edge stripe followed by a uniform suffix in the demonstrated way. Submitting the test unchanged was rejected. This disproves the assumption that the two demonstrations' simple stripe selector is sufficient to solve every fresh recurrence with this task ID, but it does not identify the correct selector or output for the fragmented test.

## Guidance

Treat the prior left-prefix/suffix rule as supported only when a fresh input actually contains the demonstrated structure. A recurring task ID is not enough to select that rule. For a fragmented pattern like this test, keep the instance unresolved and request a discriminating demo rather than extrapolating the stripe rule or guessing edits. Preserve the rejected no-op as negative evidence, not as evidence for any particular alternative transformation.

The next useful example should clarify the role of the separated patterned bands and whether the relevant object is a partial row stripe, a periodic/color pattern, or some relationship between bands. Do not claim any of these alternatives as established without additional output evidence.

## Fresh recurrence with 8 demos and 8 rejected attempts (24×25; 2026-10-21)
